blocks.markdown: **Comparative authorities only.** Bilski, Alice, KSR, Muller and Princeton are U.S. decisions. They are comparative illustrations — not binding Philippine Supreme Court doctrine. Philippine analysis begins with RA 8293.

Any technical solution of a problem in any field of human activity that is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable is patentable — whether a product, a process, or an improvement. Three cumulative elements: novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability. A patent protects a technical solution, not an abstract idea.

Excluded from patent protection: (22.1) discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods; (22.2) schemes, rules and methods of mental acts, games or business, and computer programs; (22.3) surgical, therapeutic and diagnostic methods on the human or animal body (but not products or compositions for use in them); (22.4) plant varieties, animal breeds, essentially biological production processes (but not micro-organisms or non-biological/microbiological processes); (22.5) aesthetic creations; and (22.6) anything contrary to public order or morality. Evaluate the actual claim; do not confuse a technical product or process with a disallowed abstract scheme or computer program as such.

An invention qualifies as a utility model if new and industrially applicable; Section 21 applies except for inventive step, which is not a condition. Patent requires novelty plus inventive step plus industrial applicability; utility model drops inventive step.

An industrial design is any composition of lines or colors or any three-dimensional form, with or without lines or colors, that gives a special appearance to and can serve as pattern for an industrial product or handicraft. It protects special appearance or ornamentation, not technical function.

Only new or original industrial designs are protected. Designs dictated essentially by technical or functional considerations to obtain a technical result, or contrary to public order, health or morals, are not protected. A purely functional shape is excluded.

blocks.markdown: Requisites: Sections 23–27
An invention is not new if it forms part of prior art.

Prior art is everything made available to the public anywhere in the world before the filing or priority date, plus the whole contents of qualifying earlier-filed Philippine patent, utility-model or design applications published under the Code, subject to the section's conditions. It is broad and worldwide — identify the relevant filing or priority date and earlier disclosures.

Disclosure within twelve months before filing or priority does not prejudice novelty if made by the inventor, by a patent office in specified circumstances, or by a third party who obtained the information directly or indirectly from the inventor. The grace period is limited to those sources and conditions.

An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to prior art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the filing or priority date. Ask whether a skilled person would find the claimed invention obvious on the relevant date.
An invention that can be produced and used in any industry is industrially applicable.
Ownership: Sections 28–31, 67–68

The right to a patent belongs to the inventor, his heirs or assigns; joint makers own jointly. The inventor is the original owner, subject to joint inventorship, assignment, succession and statutory rules.

Where two or more persons separately and independently made the invention, the right belongs to the filer — or, among multiple applications for the same invention, to the applicant with the earliest filing or priority date.

Commissioned work: the commissioner owns the patent unless the contract provides otherwise. Employee inventions: (a) the employee owns if inventive activity is not part of regular duties, even using employer time, facilities or materials; (b) the employer owns if the invention results from regularly assigned duties, unless otherwise agreed. Separate commissioned work from employee work, then ask whether inventive activity formed part of regular duties.

An applicant who previously applied for the same invention in a reciprocating country is treated as filing on the foreign filing date if: (a) the local application expressly claims priority; (b) it is filed within twelve months; and (c) a certified copy of the foreign application with English translation is filed within six months from Philippine filing. Priority requires the express claim and strict deadlines; do not confuse priority date with local filing date.

A person declared by final court order to own the patent right may, within three months after finality, prosecute the application, file a new application, request refusal, or seek cancellation of an issued patent. One declared by final decision the true and actual inventor may be substituted as patentee or elect cancellation, with damages if warranted. These remedies follow a final decision establishing entitlement or inventorship.
Application, filing date, grant, term and cancellation

The Filipino-or-English application contains: (a) request for grant; (b) description; (c) necessary drawings; (d) one or more claims; and (e) abstract. No patent issues unless the application identifies the inventor. The claims are central because they define the scope of protection sought.

The filing date is the Office's receipt date of at least: (a) an express or implied indication that a Philippine patent is sought; (b) information identifying the applicant; and (c) a Filipino-or-English description plus one or more claims. Filing date turns on these minimum elements; priority date is the separate Section 31 concept.

Section 50: if the application meets the Act and all fees are timely paid, the Office grants the patent, effective on publication of the grant in the IPO Gazette. Section 51: a final examiner refusal is appealable to the Director under the Act and Regulations.
A patent's term is twenty years from the application's filing date.

An interested person may petition to cancel a patent or any claim if: (a) the claimed invention is not new or patentable; (b) the patent does not clearly and completely disclose the invention for a skilled person to carry it out; or (c) the patent is contrary to public order or morality. Cancellation may be full or partial where grounds concern only some claims.

A utility model registration expires without renewal at the end of the seventh year after filing. Cancellation grounds include failure to qualify or meet registration requirements, insufficient description or claims, missing necessary drawings, or ownership by someone other than the inventor or successor.

An industrial design registration lasts five years from filing, renewable for no more than two consecutive five-year periods — a maximum of three terms, subject to renewal fees. It may be cancelled for non-registrability, lack of novelty, or subject matter extending beyond the original application, in full or in part.
Rights conferred and limitations: Sections 71–74

Product patents confer the exclusive right to restrain unauthorized making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing of the product. Process patents confer the exclusive right to restrain unauthorized use of the process and specified dealings in products obtained directly or indirectly from it. Owners may also assign, transfer by succession, and conclude licensing contracts.

Once a patented product has been put on the Philippine market by the owner or with express consent, the owner's control over subsequent use of that particular product is limited (first sale / exhaustion).

The owner may not prevent specified private non-commercial acts not significantly prejudicing economic interests; acts exclusively for experiments on the invention; qualifying individual-case medicine preparation; or use in specified foreign ships, vessels, aircraft or land vehicles temporarily or accidentally in the Philippines. Each exception is narrow and conditional.

A good-faith prior user — using the invention or having made serious preparations in an enterprise before the filing or priority date — may continue that use within the patent's territory. The right transfers only with the relevant enterprise or business.

A government agency or government-authorized third person may exploit the invention without the owner's agreement where public interest — national security, nutrition, health, or vital-sector development — so requires, or where a judicial or administrative body has found anti-competitive exploitation. Government use requires the statutory grounds and compliance with Sections 95–97 and 100–102 conditions.
Licensing and assignment: Sections 85–104

To encourage technology transfer and control IP abuses harming competition and trade, all technology transfer arrangements must comply with the Chapter. Section 85 supplies the policy and coverage; read it with the Chapter's mandatory and prohibited clauses.
Absent a contrary provision, licensing does not stop the licensor from granting further licenses to third persons or exploiting the subject matter itself.
The licensee may exploit the arrangement's subject matter during the whole term of the technology transfer arrangement, subject to the agreement and law.

The Director of Legal Affairs may grant a license without the owner's agreement to a person capable of exploiting the invention on specified grounds, including national emergency or extreme urgency; public interest in national security, nutrition, health or vital sectors; or a judicial or administrative determination of anti-competitive exploitation by the owner or licensee. Compulsory licensing is exceptional.

Safeguards: scope and duration limited to the authorized purpose; non-exclusive; generally non-assignable except with the relevant enterprise or goodwill; predominantly for the Philippine market (subject to the anti-competitive-practice exception); terminable when grounds cease and are unlikely to recur; and adequate remuneration to the patentee.

Patents and applications may be assigned, transmitted by inheritance or bequest, or licensed. The assignment, transmission or license must be in writing and recorded in the Office; it has no effect against third parties until recorded.
Infringement: Sections 76 and 84

Unauthorized making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing of a patented product or of a product obtained directly or indirectly from a patented process — or unauthorized use of a patented process — constitutes infringement. The patentee or person with right, title or interest may sue for damages, attorney's fees, litigation expenses and injunction; reasonable royalty where damages are not readily ascertainable; up to triple actual damages; and removal from commerce or destruction of infringing goods, materials and implements. Active inducement or knowing supply of a specially adapted component unsuitable for substantial non-infringing use creates contributory liability. Identify the claim and compare the accused acts to its scope.

Where infringement is repeated by the infringer or anyone in connivance after finality of judgment against the infringer, offenders face six months to three years' imprisonment and/or a P100,000–P300,000 fine, without prejudice to civil damages. The criminal action prescribes in three years from commission. This is not a generic first-offense provision — it requires repeated infringement after final judgment, or action in connivance.
